phy_ocra.16.0.summary: Energy is stored in a system in stores such as kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. When a system changes, energy moves between these stores by heating, by work done by forces (mechanically), by work done by an electric current (electrically) or by radiation. The principle of conservation of energy says energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but never created or destroyed, so the total energy of a closed system stays constant.

core.p: In physics we always describe energy changes for a **system**: an object or group of objects we choose to study. When a system changes (something moves, heats up, stretches, burns or is switched on) the way its energy is stored changes.
bullets: A **closed system** is one where no energy or matter enters or leaves; the total energy inside it stays constant.
Choosing the system carefully matters: for a falling ball, the system is the ball and the Earth (the gravitational field).
Energy changes are described as **energy moving between stores** by a **transfer pathway**.
Energy is measured in **joules (J)**; 1 kJ = 1000 J and 1 MJ = 1 000 000 J.
Energy is a quantity that can be calculated; it is not a substance or a 'thing' that flows.

callouts.p: An object or group of objects that we are considering; the energy changes inside it are what we describe.

core.p: OCR expects you to name the store energy is in before and after a change. Each store is linked to a measurable property of the system, which is WHY we can calculate the energy in it.
bullets: **Kinetic**: energy of a moving object; increases with mass and speed.
**Gravitational potential**: energy an object has because of its height in a gravitational field.
**Elastic potential**: energy in a stretched, squashed or twisted object (spring, rubber band, bow).
**Thermal (internal)**: energy of the particles of a substance; rises when temperature rises.
**Chemical**: energy stored in chemical bonds in fuels, food and batteries; released in reactions.
**Magnetic**: energy of magnets attracting or repelling.
**Electrostatic**: energy of charges attracting or repelling.
**Nuclear**: energy stored in the nucleus of atoms; released in fission, fusion and radioactive decay.

core.p: Energy moves between stores in only a few ways. In OCR mark schemes the key ones are **heating**, **work done by forces (mechanical work)** and **work done by an electric current (electrical work)**. Radiation (light, sound waves) is also a way energy can be transferred.
bullets: **Mechanically**: a force moves an object through a distance, so work is done.
**Electrically**: a current flows because a potential difference pushes charge, so the current does work.
**By heating**: energy is transferred because of a temperature difference, from hotter to cooler.
**By radiation**: waves such as light, infrared or sound carry energy away.
Whenever energy is transferred, **work is done** or **heating** happens; the two words describe the process, not the store.

callouts.p: 'Heat', 'electrical' and 'sound' are NOT stores at GCSE. Write 'transferred by heating to the thermal store', 'transferred electrically', 'transferred by sound waves'.

core.p: When a force makes an object move in the direction of the force, energy is transferred and we say **work is done**. The amount of work equals the energy transferred.
bullets: **Work done (J) = force (N) x distance moved along the line of action of the force (m)**, W = F x d.
1 joule of work is done when a force of 1 newton moves an object 1 metre (1 J = 1 N m).
If the object does not move, no work is done on it, however hard you push.
Work done against **friction** or air resistance transfers energy to the **thermal store** of the objects and surroundings, which is why rubbing hands warms them.
Lifting an object does work against gravity and increases its gravitational potential store.
Braking: the brakes do work on the wheels, transferring energy from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes.

callouts.p: Energy transferred when a force moves an object; work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force.

fig.cap: Pushing a box along the floor. The push does work on the box (energy transferred mechanically from the person's chemical store). Friction does work against the motion, transferring energy to the thermal store of the box and floor, which warm up slightly.

core.h: Work done by an electric current
core.p: When charge flows round a circuit, the electric current does work on the components, transferring energy from the chemical store of a battery (or from a power station) to other stores.
bullets: Energy transferred (J) = charge (C) x potential difference (V): E = Q x V.
Energy transferred (J) = power (W) x time (s): E = P x t.
In a motor, electrical work increases the kinetic store of the motor (and anything it lifts).
In a heater or kettle, electrical work increases the thermal store of the element and then the water.
In a resistor, the current does work against resistance, so the resistor heats up.
A higher potential difference means each coulomb of charge transfers more energy.

callouts.p: For any mains appliance, start your answer with 'energy is transferred electrically (by the current doing work) from the mains...'.

core.p: Heating transfers energy because of a **temperature difference**. Energy always moves from the hotter object to the cooler one until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).
bullets: Heating raises the energy in the **thermal store** of the cooler object and lowers it in the hotter object.
Heating can happen by conduction, convection and radiation (infrared).
Heating a substance can also change its state without a temperature change; the energy goes into breaking bonds between particles.
When a kettle boils water, the element is heated electrically, then heats the water.
The bigger the temperature difference, the faster energy is transferred by heating.

callouts.p: Energy transfer by heating is always from hotter to cooler, never the other way on its own.

fig.cap: Boiling a kettle: energy is transferred electrically (work done by the electric current) to the heating element, then by heating to the thermal store of the water. Some energy is also transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings, so it is dissipated.

core.h: The principle of conservation of energy
core.p: This is one of the most important laws in all of science. It means energy can be moved around and stored differently, but the total never changes in a closed system.
bullets: Energy **cannot be created or destroyed**; it can only be **transferred** usefully, **stored** or **dissipated**.
Total energy before = total energy after, for a closed system.
If some stores lose energy, other stores must gain exactly the same amount.
'Lost' energy is never destroyed; it has been transferred to stores we do not want, usually thermal stores of the surroundings.
This allows us to calculate unknown energies: e.g. energy wasted = energy input - useful energy output.

callouts.p: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored, or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.

core.h: Describing energy changes in common situations
core.p: Exam questions give an everyday situation and ask you to describe the changes in stores and the pathways. Use the pattern: **store before -> pathway -> store after (plus wasted store)**.
bullets: Ball thrown upwards: kinetic store decreases, gravitational potential store increases (work done against gravity).
Car braking: kinetic store of car decreases, thermal store of brakes and surroundings increases (work done by friction).
Battery-powered torch: chemical store of battery -> electrically -> light radiated and thermal store of surroundings.
Burning gas on a hob: chemical store of gas and oxygen -> by heating -> thermal store of pan and water.
Bungee jumper: GPE -> kinetic -> elastic potential store of the rope as it stretches.
Electric car accelerating: chemical store of battery -> electrically -> kinetic store of car.
Vehicle collision: kinetic store -> work done deforming the vehicles -> thermal store and sound.

fig.cap: A ball dropped from rest (ignoring air resistance). Energy in the gravitational potential store falls as energy in the kinetic store rises; the total bar length stays the same, showing conservation of energy. Work done by gravity is the transfer pathway.

core.p: In real systems some energy is always transferred to stores where it is not useful, usually the thermal store of the surroundings. We say it is **dissipated** (spread out). It is still there, but it is spread so thinly it is hard to use again.
bullets: Friction, air resistance and electrical resistance cause dissipation.
Dissipated energy warms the surroundings by a tiny amount.
Because energy spreads out, it becomes less useful even though the total is conserved.
Full treatment of dissipation and efficiency is in P7.2.

core.p: Using conservation of energy turns a description into a calculation. For a closed system, add up the energy in every store before and after; the totals must match.
bullets: If a 50 J GPE store falls to 20 J and nothing is wasted, the kinetic store has gained 30 J.
If friction is present, the gain in kinetic energy is LESS than the loss in GPE; the difference went to the thermal store.
Useful energy out + wasted energy out = total energy in.
Always state the units (J) and the stores involved.
Equations for each store (KE, GPE, elastic) are covered in P7.1d-e.

callouts.p: If your answer gives more energy out than went in, you have broken conservation of energy, so recheck.

core.p: Grade 9 answers link the store to the physical change that causes it and name the force or process doing the work.
bullets: Say WHICH force does the work: 'work is done by friction between brake pads and disc'.
Say WHICH object's store changes: 'the thermal store of the brake pads', not just 'heat'.
Separate stores from pathways in every line of a 6-mark answer.
Identify the system first, then trace each store that changes and finish with conservation: 'the total energy stays the same'.
Recognise that a pendulum or bouncing ball eventually stops because energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings by air resistance and in impacts.

callouts.p: Never write energy is 'used up', 'lost' or 'made'. Write it is transferred or dissipated.

analogy.p: Think of energy as money and each store as a different bank account (kinetic account, thermal account and so on). Transfer pathways are the ways money moves: bank transfer, cash, cheque. In a closed system no money is printed or burnt, so the total across all accounts stays the same; it only moves between accounts. Dissipation is like spreading coins thinly among thousands of strangers: the money still exists but you cannot easily get it back. It breaks down because money is a real object you can hold, whereas energy is just a number we calculate, and money can be printed, but energy can never be created.

terms.d: An object or group of objects whose energy changes are being considered.
A system where no energy or matter enters or leaves, so its total energy is constant.
A way energy is held in a system, e.g. kinetic, thermal, chemical.
Energy an object has because it is moving.
Energy an object has because of its position (height) in a gravitational field.
Energy stored in an object that has been stretched, compressed or deformed elastically.
Energy of the particles of a substance; increases when its temperature rises.
Energy stored in chemical bonds, released by chemical reactions.
Energy stored in the nuclei of atoms.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object; W = F x d.
Energy transferred when an electric current flows through a component; E = Q x V.
Energy transfer caused by a temperature difference, from hotter to cooler.
Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated but cannot be created or destroyed.
Energy spreading out to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, becoming less useful.
Unit of energy; the work done when a 1 N force moves an object 1 m.

mistakes.w: Energy is used up when a car moves.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred from the chemical store of the fuel to the kinetic store and thermal store of the surroundings; it is not used up.

mistakes.w: Heat energy and sound energy are stores.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred by heating or by sound waves; the store is the thermal store.

mistakes.w: Electrical energy is stored in the wires.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred electrically by work done by the current.

mistakes.w: Pushing a wall does work on it.
mistakes.r: No work is done because the wall does not move (distance = 0).

mistakes.w: Energy is lost to friction and disappears.
mistakes.r: Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store of the surfaces and surroundings; it is dissipated.

mistakes.w: Energy is created in a power station.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred from the chemical or nuclear store of the fuel.

mistakes.w: Heat flows from cold to hot to cool a drink.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred by heating from the hotter drink to the cooler surroundings.
A falling ball's gravitational potential store decreases and its kinetic store increases.

exam.q: State the principle of conservation of energy.
model: Energy cannot be created or destroyed (only transferred, stored or dissipated).

exam.q: Name the energy store that increases when a spring is stretched.
model: Elastic potential (store).

exam.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Describe the energy changes as it rises.
model: Energy in the kinetic store decreases.
Energy in the gravitational potential store increases (work done against gravity).
exam.tip: Give both the decreasing and increasing store.

exam.q: Name three ways energy can be transferred between stores.
model: Any three from: heating, mechanical work (by forces), electrical work (by current), radiation.
3 correct = 2 marks, 2 correct = 1 mark.

exam.q: Explain why rubbing your hands together makes them warm.
model: Work is done against friction.
Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the hands (temperature rises).

exam.q: A car brakes to a stop. Describe the energy transfers.
model: Energy in the kinetic store of the car decreases.
Work is done by friction between brake pads and discs.
Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes / surroundings (and some by sound).

exam.q: An electric kettle is switched on. Describe the energy transfers from the mains to the water.
model: Energy is transferred electrically / current does work in the heating element.
The thermal store of the element increases.
Energy is transferred by heating to the thermal store of the water (some to the surroundings).
exam.tip: Mention both electrical and heating pathways.

exam.q: A pendulum swings and eventually stops. Explain, using conservation of energy, why it stops even though energy is not destroyed.
model: Energy is transferred between gravitational potential and kinetic stores as it swings.
Work is done against air resistance (and friction at the pivot).
Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings / dissipated.
Total energy is conserved, but less remains in the pendulum's stores until none is left.
exam.tip: Always end with 'total energy stays the same'.

exam.q: A 60 J gravitational potential store of a sledge decreases to 0 J as it slides down a hill. Its kinetic store at the bottom is 45 J. Calculate the energy transferred to the thermal store and explain where it has gone.
model: Work done against friction (and air resistance).
Transferred to the thermal store of the sledge, snow and surroundings.
exam.tip: Use conservation: energy in = energy out.

exam.q: Describe the energy changes for a bungee jumper from the moment they jump to the lowest point. Refer to stores and transfers.
model: Jumper starts with energy in the gravitational potential store.
As they fall, GPE store decreases and kinetic store increases (work done by gravity).
Once the rope becomes taut, it stretches.
Kinetic store (and remaining GPE) transferred to the elastic potential store of the rope.
At the lowest point the jumper is momentarily at rest so kinetic store is zero; elastic store is maximum.
Some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings by air resistance; total energy is conserved.
exam.tip: Work in order through time and finish with conservation.

exam.q: Explain the difference between an energy store and an energy transfer, using a battery-powered fan as an example.
model: A store is where energy is held, e.g. chemical store of the battery.
A transfer is the process by which energy moves, e.g. electrically / by the current doing work.
Energy ends in the kinetic store of the fan blades (and air).
Some is transferred by heating to the thermal store of the motor / surroundings.

worked.q: A crane lifts a load, increasing its gravitational potential store by 12 000 J. The motor transfers 20 000 J electrically. How much energy is dissipated and where does it go?
steps: Conservation of energy: energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy.
This is transferred to the thermal store of the motor, cables and surroundings (and some as sound).
worked.ans: 8 000 J dissipated, mainly to thermal stores of the motor and surroundings.

worked.q: Describe the energy changes when a match is struck and burns.
steps: Striking: work is done by friction, increasing the thermal store of the match head.
The chemicals react: energy is transferred from the chemical store of the match and oxygen.
Energy is transferred by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings and by radiation (light).
Total energy is conserved; the chemical store decreases by the same amount the other stores increase.
worked.ans: Chemical store -> heating and light radiation -> thermal store of surroundings, with total energy unchanged.

worked.q: A 2 N force pushes a toy car 3 m along a table. Calculate the work done and describe the energy transfer.
steps: Energy is transferred mechanically from the chemical store of the person.
It goes to the kinetic store of the car, and some to the thermal store via friction.
worked.ans: 6 J of work done; energy transferred mechanically to the car's kinetic store and thermal stores.

phy_ocra.16.1.summary: You can calculate the energy in three key stores: kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed squared, gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height, and elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x extension squared. Using conservation of energy, the energy lost by one store equals the energy gained by others, so you can link these equations to find unknown speeds, heights and extensions. Practical work (PAG P5) checks these predictions and shows that real systems dissipate some energy.

core.p: P7.1a-c tells you WHICH stores change; this point is about HOW MUCH. Each store has an equation linking the energy to properties you can measure. Combined with conservation of energy, these let you predict speeds, heights and extensions.
bullets: **Kinetic energy**: depends on mass and speed.
**Gravitational potential energy**: depends on mass, gravitational field strength and change in height.
**Elastic potential energy**: depends on spring constant and extension.
All energies are in **joules (J)**; always convert to SI units first (kg, m, m/s, N/m).
In OCR you must **recall** the KE and GPE equations; the elastic energy equation is **given** on the equation sheet but you must be able to select and use it.

Equation (words)
Symbols
Units
rows: GPE = mass x g x height
E = 0.5 x spring constant x extension^2

core.p: Anything moving has energy in its kinetic store. The faster it moves and the more massive it is, the more energy it has.
bullets: **Kinetic energy (J) = 0.5 x mass (kg) x (speed (m/s))^2**.
KE is **directly proportional to mass**: double the mass, double the KE.
KE is **proportional to speed squared**: double the speed, four times the KE; triple the speed, nine times.
Square the speed BEFORE multiplying by 0.5 and the mass.
A stationary object has zero kinetic energy.
Rearranged: m = 2KE / v^2 and v = square root of (2KE / m).

callouts.p: 0.5 x 4 x 3^2 = 18 J, not (0.5 x 4 x 3)^2 = 36 J. Always square only the speed.

fig.cap: Kinetic energy against speed is a curve (a parabola) because KE depends on speed squared. Doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four, which is why stopping distances rise so steeply with speed.

core.p: Lifting an object does work against gravity, increasing its gravitational potential store. The energy gained depends on how far it is lifted, not on the route taken.
bullets: **Gravitational potential energy (J) = mass (kg) x gravitational field strength (N/kg) x height (m)**.
On Earth g is about 10 N/kg (OCR papers state the value to use, sometimes 9.8 N/kg).
Use the **change in vertical height**, not the distance along a slope.
GPE is directly proportional to mass, to g and to height.
On the Moon g is about 1.6 N/kg, so the same lift gives much less GPE.
Rearranged: h = GPE / (m x g); m = GPE / (g x h).

callouts.p: gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height

core.p: Stretching or compressing a spring does work on it, which is stored in its elastic potential store. This only applies while the spring obeys Hooke's law (is not stretched past its limit of proportionality).
bullets: **Energy stored in a stretched spring (J) = 0.5 x spring constant (N/m) x (extension (m))^2**.
Extension = stretched length - original length (convert cm to m!).
The spring constant k measures stiffness: a bigger k means a stiffer spring.
Energy is proportional to extension squared: double the extension, four times the energy.
The energy equals the **area under the force-extension graph**.
Past the limit of proportionality the equation no longer applies; use the area under the curve instead.

callouts.p: Force = spring constant x extension (F = kx). Use it to find k first if a question gives force and extension.

fig.cap: Left: a spring stretched by extension x. Right: a force-extension graph. Up to the limit of proportionality the line is straight (F = kx) and the area under it (a triangle, 0.5 x F x x) equals the energy in the elastic potential store, 0.5kx^2.

core.h: Using conservation of energy in calculations
core.p: In a closed system with no dissipation, the energy lost by one store equals the energy gained by another. This lets you link two equations together.
bullets: Falling object: GPE lost = KE gained, so mgh = 0.5mv^2.
Object thrown upwards: KE lost = GPE gained at the top.
Catapult: elastic energy stored = KE of the projectile (if no losses).
Pendulum: KE at the bottom = GPE gained at the highest point.
If friction or air resistance acts, KE gained < GPE lost; the difference is the energy dissipated.

callouts.p: For free fall without air resistance, mgh = 0.5mv^2 gives v = square root of (2gh): the final speed does not depend on mass.

fig.cap: Higher-tier link between stores: an object dropped from 5 m (g = 10 N/kg, no air resistance). Equating GPE lost to KE gained cancels the mass, giving v = square root of 2gh = 10 m/s whatever the mass.

core.p: Higher papers expect you to rearrange equations that contain squares and to chain two energy equations together in one problem.
bullets: From KE = 0.5mv^2: v^2 = 2KE / m, then take the square root.
From E = 0.5kx^2: x^2 = 2E / k, then take the square root.
Combine: 0.5kx^2 = 0.5mv^2 for a spring launching a mass, so v = x times square root of (k/m).
Combine: mgh = 0.5mv^2 to find the height a ball reaches: h = v^2 / 2g.
Keep at least 3 significant figures during working and round only at the end.

callouts.p: Write the equation, substitute with units, rearrange, then calculate. Each step can earn a mark even if the final answer is wrong.

core.p: Many lost marks come from units, not physics. Convert everything to SI units before substituting.
bullets: Mass in **kg**: 500 g = 0.5 kg.
Extension and height in **m**: 4 cm = 0.04 m.
Speed in **m/s**: 36 km/h = 10 m/s (divide km/h by 3.6).
Energy in **J**: 2.5 kJ = 2500 J.
Spring constant in **N/m**; g in **N/kg**.

callouts.p: If x = 5 cm, x^2 = 0.0025 m^2, not 25. Convert first, then square.

core.p: A typical practical compares the GPE lost by a trolley on a ramp with the KE it gains, showing conservation of energy and the effect of friction.
bullets: Measure the trolley mass with a balance (kg).
Measure the **vertical height** of the release point with a metre rule.
Release from rest; use a **light gate and data logger** (or card length / time) to find speed at the bottom.
Calculate GPE = mgh and KE = 0.5mv^2 and compare.
KE is usually a bit less than GPE because work is done against friction and air resistance.
Repeat each height three times and calculate a mean speed to reduce random error.
Vary the height and plot KE against GPE: ideally a straight line through the origin with gradient close to 1.

callouts.p: Light gates remove human reaction time; measure height vertically with a set square and rule.

fig.cap: A trolley released from rest at height h on a ramp. Its gravitational potential energy (mgh) is transferred to kinetic energy (0.5mv^2). A light gate measures the speed at the bottom so the two energies can be compared; any difference was dissipated by friction.

core.h: Practical: energy stored in a spring
core.p: Hang masses on a spring, measure extension, and use the force-extension graph to find k and the stored energy.
bullets: Weight added (N) = mass (kg) x 10 N/kg.
Measure the extension with a ruler at eye level (avoid parallax), using a pointer on the spring.
Plot force against extension; the gradient of the straight part = k.
Energy stored = area under the line = 0.5 x F x x = 0.5kx^2.
Do not exceed the limit of proportionality or the spring deforms permanently.
Safety: wear eye protection and keep feet clear of falling masses.

core.p: Exam questions often ask what happens to the energy when one variable changes, without numbers.
bullets: Mass doubled: KE doubles; GPE doubles.
Speed doubled: KE x 4. Speed halved: KE / 4.
Height tripled: GPE x 3.
Extension doubled: elastic energy x 4.
Spring constant doubled at same extension: elastic energy x 2.

callouts.p: Any variable that is squared in an equation has a squared effect on the answer.

core.p: These equations explain safety features and design choices.
bullets: Speed limits: a car at 60 mph has about 4 times the KE of one at 30 mph, so braking needs about 4 times the work (and distance).
Roller coasters: the first hill must be highest because GPE at the top must cover KE and losses later.
Hydroelectric dams: water stored high has a large GPE store.
Trampolines and bows store elastic energy then transfer it to kinetic.
Crumple zones transfer KE by doing work deforming the car, over a longer time.

analogy.t: A water tower and a water slide
analogy.p: Climbing to the top of a water slide is like filling a gravitational potential 'tank': the higher you climb, and the heavier you are, the more you store (mgh). Sliding down empties that tank into a kinetic 'tank' that fills faster and faster, because kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Friction with the slide is like a leak that drips some energy into warming the slide and water. The analogy breaks down because energy is not a fluid sitting in a tank, and the kinetic 'tank' does not fill in proportion to speed; it fills with speed squared.

terms.d: Energy in the kinetic store of a moving object; KE = 0.5mv^2.
Energy in the gravitational potential store due to height in a gravitational field; GPE = mgh.
Energy stored in an elastically deformed object; E = 0.5kx^2.
Amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg).
Distance travelled per unit time, in m/s.
Force of gravity on each kilogram of mass, in N/kg; about 10 N/kg on Earth.
Vertical distance moved in the gravitational field, in metres.
Force needed per metre of extension; a measure of stiffness, in N/m.
Increase in length of a spring from its original length, in metres.
Point beyond which force is no longer proportional to extension.
Extension is directly proportional to force applied, up to the limit of proportionality.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred, stored or dissipated.
A sensor that records the time an object blocks a beam, used to calculate speed.
The SI unit of energy.

mistakes.w: KE = 0.5 x m x v (forgetting to square).
mistakes.r: KE = 0.5 x m x v^2; square the speed.
Only the speed is squared, then multiplied by 0.5 and m.

mistakes.w: Using the slope length for h in GPE.
mistakes.r: Use the vertical change in height.

mistakes.w: Using total spring length instead of extension.
mistakes.r: Extension = new length - original length, in metres.

mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster so hit the ground with higher speed.
mistakes.r: Without air resistance, v = square root of 2gh, independent of mass.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the square root when finding v.
mistakes.r: After finding v^2 = 2KE/m, take the square root.

exam.q: Write down the equation linking kinetic energy, mass and speed.
model: Kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed^2.

exam.q: A 2 kg book is lifted 1.5 m. g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy.
model: GPE = 2 x 10 x 1.5

exam.q: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 70 kg cyclist moving at 8 m/s.
A spring of spring constant 40 N/m is stretched by 5 cm. Calculate the energy stored.
The speed of a car doubles. State what happens to its kinetic energy.
model: It increases by a factor of 4 (quadruples).

exam.q: A 0.2 kg ball has 10 J of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed.
model: v = 10 m/s

exam.q: A stone of mass 0.1 kg is dropped from 20 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before it hits the ground. g = 10 N/kg.
model: KE gained = GPE lost = 20 J
v = 20 m/s

exam.q: A catapult with k = 200 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m and fires a 0.02 kg stone. Calculate the maximum launch speed.
model: KE = 1 J (assuming no losses)
v = 10 m/s
exam.tip: State the assumption of no energy dissipated.

exam.q: In the ramp experiment, the calculated KE at the bottom is less than the GPE at the top. Explain why.
model: Work is done against friction / air resistance.
Some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the trolley, ramp and surroundings.

exam.q: Describe how you would carry out an experiment to show that gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy when a trolley rolls down a ramp. Include measurements and calculations.
model: Measure mass of trolley with a balance.
Measure vertical height of release point with a metre rule.
Release trolley from rest at the top.
Measure speed at the bottom using a light gate (card length / time).
Calculate GPE = mgh and KE = 0.5mv^2 and compare.
Repeat for different heights and repeat readings to find means; KE slightly less due to friction.
exam.tip: Cover method, measurements, equations and evaluation.

worked.q: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop. How much energy is transferred from its kinetic store? If it then travels at 10 m/s, how does its KE compare?
steps: Halving the speed divides KE by 4.
worked.ans: 240 000 J (240 kJ); at half the speed the KE is one quarter, 60 000 J.

worked.q: (Higher) A 0.5 kg ball is thrown upwards at 6 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 N/kg, find the maximum height it reaches.
steps: KE at launch = 0.5 x 0.5 x 6^2 = 9 J.
At the top KE = 0, so GPE gained = 9 J.

worked.q: A spring stretches from 12 cm to 20 cm when a 4 N force is applied. Find k and the energy stored.
